title: SLA-backed Dedicated Capacity: Messaging & Procurement Playbook for Platform Finance & Ops
content:
Purpose:
Quick reference and messaging for commercial and technical stakeholders (platform/ops/fin) when evaluating SLA-backed dedicated inference capacity. Emphasis on cost predictability, isolation guarantees, and procurement language that reduces buyer friction.

Intended audience:
- Platform engineering leads
- Infrastructure/ops procurement and finance
- Customer procurement/legal (for RFP responses)
- Sales / AE enablement (procurement assist)

Executive positioning (30s soundbite):
‘Redwood Dedicated delivers predictable inference economics for production LLMs — guaranteed throughput and strict tenant isolation with contract-level SLOs and clear remediation paths so your platform team can forecast cost, capacity, and compliance without building inference ops from scratch.’

Core value hypotheses (finance + ops framing):
1) Predictable unit cost: Reserved capacity converts variable per-token spend into a fixed, amortizable cost with committed throughput and burst allowances. Easier for finance to forecast and attribute.
2) Operational risk reduction: Isolation primitives (dedicated GPU pools, network segmentation, audit logs) materially reduce blast radius and accelerate incident MTTR vs. shared-hosted alternatives.
3) Procurement simplicity: Pre-canned SLA slabs and objective remediation triggers shorten negotiation cycles and reduce legal redlines.
4) Migration flexibility: Version-pinned model rollouts + fallback routing allow ops to maintain SLOs during upgrades.

What platform/ops care about (buyer pain capture):
- Unexpected token spend spikes blow budget forecasts.
- Noisy neighbors and noisy models cause tail latency and request drops.
- Lack of auditability for regulated workloads.
- Upgrades that degrade latency or throughput without easy rollback.

Differentiation vs. typical competitors (notes for competitive rebuttals):
- Public cloud managed endpoints: cheaper at face value but lack inference-specific SLA granularity (e.g., sustained throughput guarantees at 99th percentile), plus harder isolation for multi-tenant inference workloads.
- Inference infrastructure vendors (open-source runtimes + self-host): greater control but higher ops burden and delayed time-to-value; Redwood offers packaged SLAs + operational support.
- Other LLM API vendors: often provide soft promises on rate-limiting or throughput; our SLA ties to capacity allocation, burst policy, and documented fallback models.

SLA primitives to highlight (language for marketing / contract drafts):
- Throughput SLO: sustained tokens-per-second per-tenant with 99.9th percentile latency caps measured over rolling 24h windows.
- Availability SLO: percentage of time the dedicated pool accepts traffic (exclusions enumerated).
- Isolation guarantees: dedicated GPU pool, tenant-specific KV cache isolation, and VPC peering options for private deployments.
- Capacity elasticity: defined burst credits and ramp-up schedule tied to committed baseline.
- Remedies and credits: tiered credit schedule when SLOs miss (simple, transparent formula).

Procurement-ready contract language (boilerplate suggestions):
- ‘Redwood will provision and maintain a dedicated inference pool with baseline capacity of X TKS (tokens/sec) for Customer, with burst capacity of up to Y TKS subject to availability. Redwood will maintain a 99.9% availability SLO per calendar month, excluding permitted maintenance and force majeure.’
- ‘In the event of SLO miss, Customer shall be eligible for service credits calculated as a percentage of the monthly committed fee per each 0.1% below the SLO up to a cap of 50% of the monthly fee.’
- ‘Tenant isolation shall include: non-shared GPU allocation, tenant-specific network ACLs, and independent KV cache namespaces. Cross-tenant data leakage will be investigated and remediated at Redwood’s expense.’

Commercial packaging options (pricing/commit framing):
- Baseline Reserved: commit to sustained X tokens/sec for 12/36 months. Price = baseline fee + metered overage at a reduced rate.
- Reserved + Burst: baseline + explicit burst pool credits for seasonal spikes.
- Enterprise Private: on-prem/VPC with higher platform fee + premium SLA. Includes white-glove onboarding and 24x7 escalation channel.

Buyer decision choreography (sales playbook steps for procurement-heavy deals):
1) Discovery: capture budget model (monthly committed spend), peak load patterns, upgrade cadence, security/compliance requirements.
2) Capacity proposal: map historical peak to committed baseline + burst credit; include cost comparison to current per-token spend.
3) SLA preview: provide tailored SLO numbers and remediation economics.
4) Pilot/POC: short-term reserved small pool with ops runbook and test harness (latency/throughput bench).
5) Contract: use procurement-ready language above and pre-agreed operational onboarding checklist.

Operational onboarding checklist (what ops teams will ask for):
- Network diagram (VPC peering, endpoint IPs), RBAC and key provisioning, logging/audit stream subscription, model-version pinning policy, capacity escalation path, runbook for failover to fallback model, SLI dashboards definition.

Examples & quick math (to use in internal decks):
- Example customer: e-comm recommender — baseline 500 TKS, peak 2,000 TKS for 2 hours/day. Baseline reserved saves ~37% vs fully metered per-token pricing in steady state; burst credits cover 95% of peak spikes while keeping cost predictability.
- Credit calc example: monthly committed fee = $120k. If availability SLO falls by 0.5% below target, credit = 5% of monthly fee (example schedule).

Competitive risks & mitigation (honest):
- Risk: Large cloud providers may counter with custom discounts tied to broader infrastructure buys.
  Mitigation: Emphasize inference-specific optimizations (KV caching, batching) and speed to production; offer migration assistance + proof of unit economics.
- Risk: Some buyers insist on unlimited burst.
  Mitigation: Offer limited trial bursts and transparent burst pricing; surface historical utilization patterns to justify caps.

Open questions & items for legal/prod to finalize:
- Precise SLI definitions and measurement endpoints (network ingress vs. service-level TPS?).
- Maintenance windows: how to schedule and communicate to customers to minimize SLA impact.
- Negotiable credit caps for strategic accounts.

Appendix: suggested SLO numeric templates (editable)
- Latency SLO: 99th percentile generation latency <= 400ms for requests <= 512 tokens.
- Throughput SLO: baseline sustained tps = X tokens/sec (customer-specific), 99th percentile across 24h rolling window.
- Availability SLO: 99.9% uptime for the dedicated pool per month.

Notes to self / drafts bits (informal):
- Pull usage distributions from telemetry to build baseline -> sales should always show customers their own cost delta.
- Put simple one-page TCO table in the quote (reserved fee, expected metered delta, expected 12-mo saving).
- Create a short checklist for legal: SLO measurement endpoints, credit formula, escalation contacts, support hours.

References / links to internal artifacts:
- SLA template (Confluence) — linked above.
- Recent pilot telemetry: JIRA-REQ-4123 contains perf traces.

Action items:
- (Maya) Draft a one-page TCO calculator for AEs by 2025-08-15.
- (Diego) Assemble sample telemetry + bench results from two pilot customers by 2025-08-22.
- (Legal) Review suggested credit schedule and measurement endpoints by 2025-09-05.

Status: draft — needs legal SLO wording + product confirmation on measurement endpoints.

Unresolved negotiation levers to discuss with sales ops:
- Minimum monthly commitment thresholds.
- Whether to permit multi-month averaging for SLO measurement during first 90 days of onboarding.
- Cross-contract cascade: if Dedicated pool serves multiple regions, how to apportion credits.

End of doc.
